notes:
Below are notes on Job 36, verse by verse. I used Enduring Word (David Guzik), the Pulpit Commentary, Wesley's Notes, Clarke, Matthew Henry, Jamieson-Fausset-Brown (JFB), Coffman, the Preacher's Homiletical Commentary, Bible Hub's summary, the NET and NLT translations, and two Desiring God pieces.

**What I couldn't find:**
- The NET Bible's translator notes for this chapter (I only saw its translation).
- Gill and Ellicott.
- Any page on newadvent.org, catholic.com or oca.org about this chapter.
- Anything from prosperity, word-of-faith or hyper-grace teachers on this chapter.
- The Catholic voices that do appear (Gregory, Aquinas) come second-hand, through a Protestant writer.

## Background: the big question is Elihu himself

Writers disagree less over single verses than over whether Elihu speaks for God. That decides how you read every verse.

- **He's mostly wrong (Enduring Word):** Guzik's summary says that if Job obeyed, God would lift him into richness and freedom, "yet chapters 1–2 make clear Elihu is absolutely wrong." Guzik does see a change of tone from v. 22 on. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/job-36/
- **He's a false teacher (Coffman, a Churches of Christ commentator):** Coffman opens with "No speech with an evil purpose is a good speech, regardless of the content of it." https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/bcc/job-36.html
- **He's nearer the truth than the three friends (Pulpit Commentary):** Elihu sees suffering as more about correction than punishment. That is "not exactly the truth" but "far nearer the truth" than the friends' view. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/job-36.html
- **Matthew Henry agrees:** the friends said Job suffered because he was wicked. Elihu said the trouble was a trial that went on because Job hadn't yet been fully humbled. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/mhc/Job/Job_036.cfm
- **JFB says the same:** for the godly, suffering is discipline. It continues not because of great guilt, as the friends claimed, but because the discipline hasn't done its work yet. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/jfb/Job/Job_036.cfm
- **He's right (Reformed and Baptist voices at Desiring God):**
  - John Piper: Elihu teaches something Job and his friends never found. The suffering of the righteous is "a token of God's… love," not of his anger. https://www.desiringgod.org/messages/job-rebuked-in-suffering
  - Christopher Ash now holds that Elihu "speaks by inspiration of the Spirit as a true and prophetic voice." He admits eleven of the twelve Job commentaries he owns think poorly of Elihu. https://www.desiringgod.org/articles/let-the-youth-speak
- **Historic voices, as reported by Ash** (same URL as above):
  - Gregory the Great and Thomas Aquinas both thought Elihu's teaching was sound but faulted him for pride or seeking glory.
  - Calvin had nothing bad to say about him. A scholar Ash quotes says Calvin treats Elihu as "a true doctor of the church."
- **Modern scholarship, as reported by Ash** (same URL): since 1804 many critics have treated chapters 32–37 as added later, though no manuscript supports this. Some find Elihu pompous, or even comic relief.

## Verse by verse

**v. 1:** This begins Elihu's fourth speech. Chapters 36 and 37 are one speech and shouldn't have been split in the middle of a thunderstorm. It is a last appeal to Job to submit and be patient. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/job-36.html

**v. 2:**
- Literally "there are yet words for God": the case on God's behalf isn't closed yet. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/job-36.html
- Guzik thinks Elihu sensed his hearers were tiring. He also notes that Elihu claims to speak for God, while the other friends leaned on traditional wisdom. Spurgeon joked about the promise of brevity: Elihu says "suffer me a little," then fills two more chapters. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/job-36/

**v. 3:**
- **Wesley (Methodist):** "from afar" means drawing on distant times, places and things. Elihu will defend God from the works of creation and providence, not just from Job's case. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/wes/job/36.htm
- **Clarke** agrees: the end of the chapter shows the knowledge comes from all of creation. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/acc/job-36.html
- **Pulpit:** what follows doesn't live up to the grand introduction. Elihu's arguments are mostly "trite and commonplace." https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/job-36.html
- **Coffman:** "ascribe righteousness" really means Job is getting what he deserves. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/bcc/job-36.html

**v. 4: who is "perfect in knowledge"?**
- **God:** Guzik thinks it probably means God. He cites Smick and Bullinger, who points to 37:16, where the same phrase clearly describes God. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/job-36/
- **Wesley** also reads it as God: "Thou hast to do with a God of perfect knowledge." https://biblehub.com/commentaries/wes/job/36.htm
- **Elihu himself:** the Pulpit Commentary says plainly that he speaks of himself. It suggests he may only be promising to speak truthfully. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/job-36.html
- **Translations split too:** the NLT has "I am a man of great knowledge." https://www.blueletterbible.org/nlt/job/36/1/
- **A charismatic angle:** Guzik quotes Mason, who calls this "the charismatic paradox." Elihu may have a real prophetic gift, but revelation doesn't make anyone perfect in knowledge. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/job-36/

**v. 5:**
- Guzik quotes Meyer: God despises no one *because* he is so great. Spurgeon says God's greatness of soul is the very reason he despises no one. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/job-36/
- JFB: God's might lies in his understanding, which searches out the smallest things so each person gets what is right. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/jfb/Job/Job_036.cfm
- Wesley: God's strength is guided by wisdom, so it can't do anything unjust to his creatures. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/wes/job/36.htm
- Clarke reads it as God not scolding anyone for lacking knowledge, and links it to James 1:5. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/acc/job-36.html
- The NET translates "firm in his intent." https://www.blueletterbible.org/net/job/36/1/

**v. 6:**
- Pulpit: God gives the wicked no special protection, against Job's claims in 21:7. The poor and humble are God's "special charge." https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/job-36.html
- Matthew Henry: "If men will not right the injured poor, God will." https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/mhc/Job/Job_036.cfm

**v. 7:**
- Pulpit: this answers Job's longing in 29:2. Examples are Joseph, Mordecai and Daniel. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/job-36.html
- Guzik: since Job had felt God had taken his eyes off him, Elihu is quietly counting Job among the wicked. Andersen hears an echo of the Joseph story. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/job-36/

**vv. 8–10:**
- Pulpit: even when the righteous are in chains, God watches over them and measures out suffering to reform them. "Their work" means their faults. The sin named is pride, which especially tempts outwardly good people. Pulpit sees this correcting purpose as "the especial merit" of Elihu's view. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/job-36.html
- Wesley: good people too easily misuse power and prosperity. "Opens their ear" means God inclines them to listen to what he says "by the rod." https://biblehub.com/commentaries/wes/job/36.htm
- Matthew Henry: true penitents make their sins heavier in their own eyes, not lighter. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/mhc/Job/Job_036.cfm
- Coffman reads v. 9 as Elihu setting himself up as God's agent to remind Job of sins Job must have forgotten. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/bcc/job-36.html

**v. 11: obedience and prosperity (the closest the sources come to the prosperity question)**
- **Pulpit:** the old covenant often promised prosperity to the righteous. Under the new covenant such promises are carefully hedged (Mark 10:30), and believers are told to expect trouble (John 16:33; Acts 14:22). https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/job-36.html
- **Clarke (Methodist):** there may seem to be exceptions, but the promise comes true "literally or spiritually" for every true follower of God. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/acc/job-36.html
- **Bible Hub** observes that Elihu paints obedience as "the gateway to prosperity." https://biblehub.com/job/36.htm
- **Coffman:** Elihu means "confess, and you'll prosper." https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/bcc/job-36.html

**v. 12:**
- Pulpit: "the sword" is God's judgment in many forms, not necessarily a real sword. "Without knowledge" means either unaware of coming death or stubbornly ignorant of why God was correcting them. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/job-36.html
- The NET has "they pass over the river of death." https://www.blueletterbible.org/net/job/36/1/

**v. 13:**
- Pulpit links "heap up wrath" to Romans 2:5. The godless don't cry to God when first bound, so his anger keeps growing. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/job-36.html
- Matthew Henry: hypocrisy lives in the heart. Many are saints in appearance and words but "hypocrites in heart." https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/mhc/Job/Job_036.cfm
- Guzik: Elihu thought Job was a hypocrite for denying his guilt. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/job-36/

**v. 14:**
- Pulpit: literally "their soul dies in youth." The "unclean" are explained by Deuteronomy 23:17. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/job-36.html
- Clarke's Hebrew note (via Guzik): the word means shrine prostitutes, people "consecrated" to Baal and Ashtaroth. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/job-36/
- Coffman: this reflects how short the lives of Canaanite cult prostitutes usually were. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/bcc/job-36.html
- Wesley adds a spiritual reading: after death they live among unclean spirits. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/wes/job/36.htm

**v. 15:**
- Pulpit: "by" their affliction (not just "in" it). Suffering works like medicine and becomes the very means of rescue (Psalm 119:67, 71; Hebrews 12:11). https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/job-36.html
- Piper: for the righteous, suffering is "not punitive but curative." https://www.desiringgod.org/messages/job-rebuked-in-suffering

**v. 16: two readings**
- **Most older commentators: "God would have."** Wesley: "If thou hadst opened thine ear." https://biblehub.com/commentaries/wes/job/36.htm
- **Ewald, Dillmann and Cook: "God did."** The verse describes what really happened: Job's great prosperity drew him away from listening. Pulpit keeps the "would have" reading. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/job-36.html
- The NET also reads it as past fact: "he drew you." https://www.blueletterbible.org/net/job/36/1/
- The NLT says the Hebrew here is uncertain. https://www.blueletterbible.org/nlt/job/36/1/

**v. 17:**
- Guzik: Elihu "could not be clearer," and chapters 1–2 show he was "absolutely wrong." https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/job-36/
- Clarke: "Elihu is not a whit behind Job's other friends." None of them knew God had allowed Satan to afflict an innocent man. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/acc/job-36.html
- Wesley: Job had taken the side of wicked men's complaints against God. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/wes/job/36.htm
- The Preacher's Homiletical Commentary sees Elihu viewing Job as a righteous man who has sinned and is being lovingly corrected. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/phc/job-36.html

**v. 18:**
- Pulpit: the Hebrew is "exceedingly obscure," with three or four proposed renderings. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/job-36.html
- Its sermon notes apply it to Christ: only one Ransom can turn aside judgment. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/job-36.html
- The NET reads it as a bribe that "entices you with riches." The NLT offers anger leading to mockery as an alternative and says the meaning is uncertain. https://www.blueletterbible.org/net/job/36/1/ and https://www.blueletterbible.org/nlt/job/36/1/

**v. 19:**
- Pulpit: will your riches keep you out of trouble? Nothing stands against God's blow. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/job-36.html
- Guzik: Elihu wrongly assumed Job trusted in his wealth. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/job-36/

**v. 20:**
- Pulpit: this targets Job's repeated wish to die (6:9; 7:15). Wishing for death shows he hasn't fully accepted God's will. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/job-36.html
- Clarke: leave death to God. Many long for it without being ready to meet him. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/acc/job-36.html

**v. 21:**
- Wesley: Job chose to quarrel with God rather than quietly submit. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/wes/job/36.htm
- Pulpit: the charge has some basis but goes too far, and is harsher than God's own verdict (38:2; 42:7). https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/job-36.html
- Guzik: Elihu was demanding that Job give up his integrity. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/job-36/
- The NET reads differently: "because of this you have been tested by affliction." https://www.blueletterbible.org/net/job/36/1/

**v. 22:**
- Cook (in Pulpit) calls "Who is a teacher like Him?" the key note of Elihu's whole speech. God's whole government of the world is a series of moral lessons. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/job-36.html
- Wesley: God teaches through the Bible and through his Son. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/wes/job/36.htm
- **Change of tone:** Guzik sees Elihu change here as a storm approaches. He quotes Mason, who says Elihu now speaks "by the unction of the Holy Spirit." https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/job-36/

**v. 23:**
- Pulpit: Job hadn't quite said "You have done wrong," but came close (9:24; 10:3). https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/job-36.html
- Restoration Commentary: Job never said this, so he's being accused of things he didn't do. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/onr/job-36.html
- Pulpit's sermon notes conclude that God can in no sense be the author of sin. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/job-36.html

**vv. 24–25:**
- Pulpit: instead of complaining, Job should praise God's work, even in his own suffering. People near and far are watching him. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/job-36.html
- Restoration Commentary: unknown to Elihu, Satan and the angels were watching too. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/onr/job-36.html
- Wesley: God's works are so plain that anyone who isn't dull must see them. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/wes/job/36.htm

**v. 26:**
- Pulpit: this is Elihu's final lesson. However much we know of God, there's more we don't. His eternal existence is beyond us. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/job-36.html
- Guzik calls this Elihu's truest argument, though wrongly applied to Job. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/job-36/

**vv. 27–28:**
- Pulpit: God draws up moisture by the sun's heat, forms clouds, and sends rain, all for people's good. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/job-36.html
- Wesley: rain falls in drops, not in floods, in a constant cycle. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/wes/job/36.htm
- Guzik: the description was so advanced that some wrongly concluded Job was written later. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/job-36/
- The NET notes on Genesis 2:6 say the word "mist" was traditionally translated from this verse, but a related Akkadian word means underground springs. https://bible.org/sites/bible.org/resources/download/netbible/ondemand/bybook/gen.pdf

**v. 29:**
- Pulpit: "pavilion" is the sky as God's tent (Psalm 18:11), and its noise is thunder. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/job-36.html
- Wesley gives the example of a cloud as small as a man's hand spreading over the whole sky. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/wes/job/36.htm

**v. 30:** Pulpit: lightning lights the whole sky. "Covers the depths of the sea" is exaggeration for effect. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/job-36.html

**v. 31:**
- Pulpit: the same clouds bring judgment (floods, lightning) and harvest. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/job-36.html
- The NLT's alternative is "he governs." https://www.blueletterbible.org/nlt/job/36/1/

**v. 32:**
- Pulpit: the KJV's "commandeth it not to shine" is "wholly indefensible." It should read that God commands the lightning to strike its mark. Pulpit compares Assyrian and Greek gods pictured hurling thunderbolts. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/job-36.html
- Wesley follows the KJV: clouds veil the sun. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/wes/job/36.htm

**v. 33:**
- **The usual reading:** cattle sense the storm coming. Wesley says they seek shelter by instinct. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/wes/job/36.htm Coffman pictures cattle heading for shelter. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/bcc/job-36.html
- **Pulpit's reading:** even the cattle sense God riding on the storm. It calls the Revised Version's rendering "very weak." https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/job-36.html
- The NLT says the Hebrew is uncertain. https://www.blueletterbible.org/nlt/job/36/1/
- Pulpit suggests the storm that breaks in 38:1, when God speaks, was already gathering. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/job-36.html
